haiku-low.q1: They see the generic reply: "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." Nothing is stored or sent.
haiku-low.q2: The API returns the generic reply. No link is created and no email is sent.
haiku-low.q3: A link works for 30 minutes and only once. Issuing a newer link for the account, or using it, ends it sooner.
haiku-low.q4: The link stays unused and still works until it expires. The form shows the reason the password failed.
haiku-low.q5: No devices stay logged in; every session for the user is deleted, including the resetting device. The user is sent to the login page and must log in again.
haiku-low.q6: The worker retries up to 3 times with backoff, then logs the failure and drops the email. The user is not told.
haiku-low.q7: The token is created and only its SHA-256 hash is stored. The raw token is put inside the link in the queued email job.
haiku-low.q8: It hashes the token from the link and looks for a row with that hash that is unused and not expired.
haiku-low.q9: NOT STATED. The document only says the limit is 3 links per account in any rolling hour.
haiku-low.q10: Earlier unused links for that account are marked as used, before the new token is created.
haiku-low.q11: In one transaction: the link is marked used, the new password hash is saved, and all the user's sessions are deleted. The confirmation email is queued after the transaction.
haiku-low.q12: The transaction marks the link used only if it is still unused, so only one submit can succeed. The document gives no further locking detail.

sonnet.q1: The generic reply: "If an account exists for that address, we've sent a link." Nothing is stored or sent.
sonnet.q2: The limit is 3 links per account per rolling hour, so the fourth request gets the generic reply. No link is made and no email is sent.
sonnet.q3: A link is valid for 30 minutes and works once. It ends sooner if it is used (burned) or if a newer link is issued for the account, which immediately ends any earlier unused link.
sonnet.q4: Still unused and valid. The form shows the reason, and the link works until it expires.
sonnet.q5: None. Every sessions row for the user is deleted, including the device that made the reset. The user is redirected to the login page and must log in with the new password. They are not logged in automatically.
sonnet.q6: The worker retries up to 3 times with backoff, then logs the failure and drops the job. The user is not told and nobody is notified. The user can request again if under the limit.
sonnet.q7: When the token is created, the API puts the link containing the raw token into the email job on the queue, and the worker sends it. This means the queue job holds the raw token until it is sent (listed as an open question). The document does not say more about how the link is built.
sonnet.q8: The page takes the token from the link and hashes it. It looks for a reset_tokens row with that hash that is unused and not expired. If found it shows the new-password form. Otherwise it shows the expired message. Nothing changes in the database.
sonnet.q9: NOT STATED. The document says the limit is 3 links created per account in a rolling hour, but not where the count is kept or how old requests drop out.
sonnet.q10: During the request step, when a new link is requested and the account is not rate limited, any earlier unused link for that account is marked as used. This happens before the new token is created and stored.
sonnet.q11: In one database transaction: the link is marked used (only if still unused), the new password hash is saved in users, and all of the user's sessions rows are deleted. The confirmation email is queued after the transaction, followed by the redirect to login.
sonnet.q12: The transaction marks the link as used only if it is still unused, so only one of the two submits can succeed. The other gets the expired page.
